focusSummary: Austrian bakery & market staples (Semmel, Erdäpfel, Paradeiser, Jause), Beisl classics (Schweinsbraten, Apfelstrudel), compound food roots, and spoken euro prices.

lessonSteps.heading: At the Bakery Counter: die Semmel & die Jause
lessonSteps.explanation: Step into an Austrian Bäckerei at 8:00 AM and the number-one word you'll hear is die Semmel (plural: Semmeln)—the crisp, golden star-folded Kaisersemmel roll (called das Brötchen across most of Germany). Mid-morning or on an Alpine hike, Austrians enjoy die Jause: a savory snack spread of rolls, cheese, and cured ham.
lessonSteps.scenarioPrompt: You order two fresh rolls for a hiking snack at a Salzburg bakery counter.
lessonSteps.nativeText: Grüß Gott! Zwei frische Semmeln für die Jause, bitte.
lessonSteps.translation: Good day! Two fresh bread rolls for our snack break, please.
lessonSteps.literalBreakdown: Grüß Gott (good day) · Zwei frische Semmeln (two fresh rolls) · für die Jause (for the savory snack break) · bitte (please)

standardGermanVariant.nativeText: Guten Tag! Zwei frische Brötchen für die Zwischenmahlzeit, bitte.
standardGermanVariant.note: Germany uses das Brötchen for a bread roll and die Zwischenmahlzeit (or Pausenbrot / Brotzeit in Bavaria) instead of Austrian Jause.

lessonSteps.usageTip: Want a warm slice of savory meatloaf tucked inside your roll? Ask at any Austrian deli counter for 'eine Leberkässemmel'!

lessonSteps.heading: Market Produce & Compound Roots: Erd·äpfel & Paradeiser
lessonSteps.explanation: Two beloved Austrian market words reveal poetic compound roots: potatoes are die Erd·äpfel ('earth-apples', DE: die Kartoffeln), and tomatoes are die Paradeiser (from 'paradise-apples', DE: die Tomaten).
lessonSteps.scenarioPrompt: Reading handwritten wooden signs at Vienna's Naschmarkt produce stalls.
lessonSteps.nativeText: Frische Erdäpfel aus dem Waldviertel und reife Paradeiser.
lessonSteps.translation: Fresh potatoes from the Waldviertel region and ripe tomatoes.
lessonSteps.literalBreakdown: Frische Erd·äpfel (fresh earth-apples = potatoes) · und reife Paradeiser (and ripe tomatoes)

standardGermanVariant.note: In Germany, Kartoffeln and Tomaten are universal; in Austria you will encounter Erdäpfel (e.g. Erdäpfelsalat) and Paradeiser on every traditional Beisl menu.

lessonSteps.usageTip: Notice the umlaut shift in the plural root: der Apfel ('apple') -> die Äpfel ('apples') -> die Erdäpfel ('potatoes').

lessonSteps.heading: Beisl Classics & Linking Sounds: Schweins·braten & Apfel·strudel
lessonSteps.explanation: Austrian compounds frequently insert a smooth linking -s- (Fugen-s) where northern German uses -e-: Austria's crispy roast pork is der Schweins·braten (DE: der Schweinebraten). For dessert, der Apfel·strudel ('apple-whirlpool', named for its spiral pastry layers!) needs no linking letter at all.
lessonSteps.scenarioPrompt: Checking the daily lunch blackboard outside a traditional Viennese Beisl.
lessonSteps.nativeText: Mittagsmenü: Knuspriger Schweinsbraten mit Erdäpfelknödel — und danach ein warmer Apfelstrudel.
lessonSteps.translation: Lunch menu: Crispy roast pork with potato dumplings — and afterward a warm apple strudel.
lessonSteps.literalBreakdown: Schweins·braten (pork-roast) · mit Erd·äpfel·knödel (with potato-dumplings) · Apfel·strudel (apple-whirlpool pastry)

standardGermanVariant.nativeText: Mittagsmenü: Knuspriger Schweinebraten mit Kartoffelklößen — und danach ein warmer Apfelstrudel.
standardGermanVariant.note: Notice THREE regional shifts in one dish: Schweinsbraten (AT) vs. Schweinebraten (DE), Erdäpfel (AT) vs. Kartoffel (DE), and Knödel (AT/Bavaria) vs. Klöße (central/northern DE)!

lessonSteps.usageTip: Once you spot Fugen-s in Schweinsbraten, you'll recognize it in Rind·s·suppe (AT beef broth; DE: Rinderbrühe) too!

lessonSteps.heading: Spoken Euro Prices: Was macht das? — Drei Euro achtzig!
lessonSteps.explanation: At counters and markets, locals ask 'Was macht das, bitte?' ('What does that come to?') and drop the word 'Cent' completely in spoken prices: €3.80 is simply 'drei Euro achtzig'. Notice also how two-digit numbers read ones-before-tens: 85 = fünf·und·achtzig ('five-and-eighty').
lessonSteps.scenarioPrompt: Paying for two Semmeln and an Apfelstrudel slice at the bakery.
lessonSteps.nativeText: „Was macht das, bitte?“ — „Das macht vier Euro fünfzig, bitte schön.“
lessonSteps.translation: 'How much does that come to, please?' — 'That comes to four euros fifty, here you go.'
lessonSteps.literalBreakdown: Was macht das (what makes that) · vier Euro fünfzig (four euros fifty [€4.50])
lessonSteps.usageTip: To avoid mixing up 'zwei' (2) and 'drei' (3) in noisy markets, cashiers often say 'zwo' for two ('zwo Euro fünfzig' = €2.50)!

drills.prompt: You see 'Erdäpfelsalat mit Paradeisern' on a Viennese Beisl menu. What dish is that?
drills.explanation: In Austrian German, Erdäpfel means potatoes (DE: Kartoffeln) and Paradeiser means tomatoes (DE: Tomaten).

drills.prompt: At a Salzburg bakery counter you want three fresh bread rolls. Which phrase sounds like a local?
drills.cue: Austrian word for crusty bread rolls (plural)
drills.explanation: Die Semmel (plural: die Semmeln) is the standard Austrian word for a bread roll (Standard German: das Brötchen -> drei frische Brötchen).

drills.prompt: The market vendor weighs your apples and says: 'Das macht drei Euro fünfundachtzig, bitte.' Which price appears on the scale?
drills.explanation: German two-digit numbers state the ones digit before the tens digit: fünf·und·achtzig = 85, so 'drei Euro fünfundachtzig' is €3.85.

gradedStories.title: Samstagvormittag am Bauernmarkt
gradedStories.titleTranslation: Saturday Morning at the Farmers' Market
gradedStories.setting: 9:00 AM among colorful stalls at a Saturday farmers' market in Vienna

paragraphs.nativeText: Am Samstag geht Nora mit einem Stoffbeutel auf den Bauernmarkt. Zuerst kauft sie beim Bäcker vier knusprige Semmeln und einen warmen Apfelstrudel für die Jause.
paragraphs.translation: On Saturday Nora walks to the farmers' market with a cloth tote bag. First she buys four crispy bread rolls and a warm apple strudel for a snack break at the baker's.

segments.regionalNote: AT: die Semmeln · DE: die Brötchen.
AT: die Jause · DE: die Zwischenmahlzeit / Brotzeit.

paragraphs.nativeText: Danach steht sie vor einem Gemüsestand. Dort liegen gelbe Erdäpfel und rote Paradeiser in Holzkisten. „Was macht das zusammen, bitte?“, fragt Nora. „Sechs Euro vierzig, bitte schön!“, sagt die Bäuerin.
paragraphs.translation: Afterward she stands in front of a vegetable stall. Yellow potatoes and red tomatoes lie there in wooden crates. 'How much does that come to altogether, please?' asks Nora. 'Six euros forty, please!' says the farmer.

paragraphs.nativeText: Zu Mittag trifft Nora ihren Bruder im Beisl neben dem Markt. Auf der Tafel steht heute: „Frischer Schweinsbraten um zwölf Euro neunzig.“
paragraphs.translation: At lunchtime Nora meets her brother in the bistro next to the market. Today's chalkboard reads: 'Fresh roast pork for twelve euros ninety.'

segments.regionalNote: In Austria, 'um 12 Euro' ('for €12') is idiomatic alongside 'für 12 Euro'!

questions.question: What does Nora buy at the baker's first?
options: Four crispy bread rolls (Semmeln) and a warm apple strudel
Two train tickets and a coffee
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: 'Zuerst kauft sie beim Bäcker vier knusprige Semmeln und einen warmen Apfelstrudel für die Jause.'

questions.question: How much does Nora pay at the vegetable stall for her Erdäpfel and Paradeiser?
questions.explanation: The farmer replies: 'Sechs Euro vierzig, bitte schön!' (€6.40).

questions.question: Notice the Austrian preposition on the Beisl chalkboard: 'Frischer Schweinsbraten um zwölf Euro neunzig.' What does 'um' mean here?
questions.explanation: In Austrian German, 'um + price' ('um zwölf Euro neunzig') is the idiomatic way to express 'for €12.90' (DE: 'für zwölf Euro neunzig').
